sectionTitle: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.4

specStatements.text: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
energy transferred, E, in joules, J
work done, W, in joules, J
An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt.

Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the definition of power eg comparing two electric motors that both lift the same weight through the same height but one does it faster than the other.

scopeNotes.statement: power = (energy transferred)/(time) [P = E/t] power = (work done)/(time) [P = W/t]
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only these two relationships (and their direct rearrangements E = Pt, W = Pt, t = E/P) are used. No other power relationship is introduced here — there is no use of power = force × velocity, no efficiency calculation, and no kilowatt-hour work, because 4.1.1.4 states power only in terms of energy transferred or work done divided by time.

Every power value in this material is quoted in watts and every energy value in joules, with time in seconds, exactly as the section specifies. Multiples such as kilowatts and megawatts are not used, so no unit is introduced that the section does not name.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the definition of power eg comparing two electric motors that both lift the same weight through the same height but one does it faster than the other.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The comparison examples stay at the level the statement sets: the work done is either given directly or stated to be equal for the two machines, and only the time differs. Students are never asked here to calculate the work of lifting from force and distance, or from a change in gravitational potential energy — those belong to other sections of the specification, not to 4.1.1.4.

concepts.definition: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done. It is not the amount of energy transferred; it is how much is transferred each second.

A rate is an amount divided by the time taken. Because power is a rate, two machines that transfer the same energy have different powers if they take different times: the shorter the time, the greater the power.

Power can be found either from the energy transferred or from the work done, because work done is a transfer of energy. Both are measured in joules, so both give a power in watts when divided by the time in seconds.
power = (energy transferred)/(time). This word equation is one students are expected to recall and use, with energy in joules and time in seconds giving power in watts.
The symbol form of the energy version of the power equation, where P is power, E is the energy transferred and t is the time taken.
power = (work done)/(time). Used whenever a machine is described as doing work — for example a motor lifting a load — with work done in joules and time in seconds.
The symbol form of the work version of the power equation, where P is power, W is the work done and t is the time taken. Here the letter W is the quantity work done, not the unit watt.
The unit of power. Power is given the symbol P and is measured in watts, W.
The energy moved from one store to another, given the symbol E and measured in joules, J.
The time over which the transfer happens, given the symbol t and measured in seconds, s. Times given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before the power equation is used.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object, given the symbol W and measured in joules, J — the same unit as energy transferred.
An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt. So a 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second.

Two electric motors that lift the same weight through the same height do the same work. If one does it faster, it does that work in less time, so by power = (work done)/(time) it has the greater power. This is the standard example that illustrates the definition of power.
From P = E/t it follows that E = P × t and t = E/P. So energy transferred is power multiplied by time in seconds, and the time taken is the energy divided by the power.

misconceptions.question: Is a more powerful device simply one that transfers more energy?
misconceptions.correct: A more powerful device transfers energy at a greater rate — more joules every second. Over a whole job it may transfer the same total energy, or even less.
misconceptions.misconception: Power just means how much energy something transfers — the bigger the energy, the bigger the power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'powerful' means 'big' or 'strong', and energy and power are both introduced with the word 'transfer'. The time in the denominator is easy to forget.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition as a rate: power = (energy transferred)/(time). Two values are always needed, an energy and a time. A device transferring 1000 J in 1 s has a power of 1000 W; the same 1000 J spread over 100 s is only 10 W.

misconceptions.question: Two motors lift the same load through the same height, but one takes much longer. Is the slower one working harder, and so more powerful?
misconceptions.correct: The faster motor is the more powerful one. Both do the same work, but the faster motor does it in less time, so its work done ÷ time is larger.
misconceptions.misconception: The motor that keeps going for longer is doing more, so it must be the more powerful motor.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'longer time' with 'more effort'. Dividing by a larger time is counter-intuitive when the same word — 'more' — is attached to both the time and the power.
misconceptions.correction: Put numbers in. Both motors do 6000 J of work. One takes 10 s: P = 6000/10 = 600 W. The other takes 30 s: P = 6000/30 = 200 W. Same work, longer time, smaller power.

misconceptions.question: What unit is power measured in?
misconceptions.correct: Power, P, is measured in watts, W. Joules, J, are the unit of energy transferred and of work done.
misconceptions.misconception: Power is measured in joules, because power is about energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power is calculated from an energy, so the energy unit is the one students have just been using and it carries over into the answer line.
misconceptions.correction: The division changes the unit: joules divided by seconds gives watts. Always finish a power calculation by writing W, and reserve J for E and W (work done).

misconceptions.question: In the equation P = W/t, what does the letter W mean?
misconceptions.correct: W is the work done, measured in joules. The unit watt also uses the letter W, but that is the unit of P, not the quantity on the top of the fraction.
misconceptions.misconception: P = W/t must mean power = watts divided by time, since W is the symbol for the watt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification uses W for two different things in the same section: the unit watt for power, and the quantity work done. Nothing in the letter itself distinguishes them.
misconceptions.correction: Check the units line of the equation: work done, W, in joules, J; power, P, in watts, W. In the fraction W is a quantity in joules; the watt only appears in the answer.

misconceptions.question: A machine transfers 6000 J in 2 minutes. Can 2 be substituted straight into P = E/t?
misconceptions.correct: No. Time must be in seconds, so t = 120 s and P = 6000/120 = 50 W.
misconceptions.misconception: You can use whatever time unit the question gives, so 6000 ÷ 2 = 3000 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is the one in front of the student, and the conversion is an extra step that is easy to skip under time pressure.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states time, t, in seconds, s. Convert first: multiply minutes by 60, hours by 3600. Writing 't = 2 × 60 = 120 s' as a separate line before substituting makes the slip much less likely.

misconceptions.question: Should the energy transferred be multiplied by the time to find power?
misconceptions.correct: No — power is energy transferred divided by time: P = E/t.
misconceptions.misconception: Power = energy × time, because a device running for longer builds up more power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Multiplying is the more familiar operation, and students confuse this equation with E = P × t, which is its rearrangement.
misconceptions.correction: Test it with the unit: a power must come out in watts, which are joules per second, so the seconds must be underneath. Multiplying would give joule seconds, which is not a unit of power.

misconceptions.question: What does a power of 1 watt tell you?
misconceptions.correct: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt — 1 J every second, for as long as the transfer continues.
misconceptions.misconception: A power of 1 W means a total of 1 J of energy has been transferred.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase '1 joule per second' is often shortened to '1 joule' in speech and notes, and the 'per second' part is what carries the whole meaning.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the words 'each second' attached. A 1 W device transfers 1 J in the first second, 2 J in two seconds, 60 J in a minute.

misconceptions.question: Two machines do exactly the same work. Must they have the same power?
misconceptions.correct: Only if they take the same time. Equal work done in different times means different powers.
misconceptions.misconception: Same job, same work done, so the power must be the same too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The work done is the quantity the question makes obvious, and if only one number is noticed it is treated as if it settled the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Power needs both numbers. 12 000 J in 20 s is 600 W; the same 12 000 J in 60 s is 200 W. The work being equal is exactly what makes the time the deciding factor.

misconceptions.question: Are work done and energy transferred measured in different units?
misconceptions.correct: No. Work done, W, is in joules, J, and energy transferred, E, is in joules, J. That is why power can be written either as P = E/t or as P = W/t.
misconceptions.misconception: Work done is a different sort of quantity from energy, so it must have its own unit — probably newtons or watts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two symbols, two word equations and two names suggest two different quantities, and work is first met alongside forces measured in newtons.
misconceptions.correction: Doing work is a way of transferring energy, so both are measured in joules. Whichever of the two equations a question points to, the top line is a number of joules.

misconceptions.question: Does a device with a higher power always transfer more energy in total?
misconceptions.correct: No. It transfers more energy each second, but the total also depends on how long it runs, since E = P × t.
misconceptions.misconception: The higher-power device must use more energy overall, whatever happens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power and total energy are both described as 'bigger' for stronger appliances, and the running time is usually not stated in the same sentence.
misconceptions.correction: Compare a 2000 W heater for 10 s (20 000 J) with a 100 W lamp for 600 s (60 000 J). The lower-power device has transferred more energy, because it ran for much longer.

misconceptions.question: Does the power of a device tell you how long an energy transfer lasts?
misconceptions.correct: No. Power tells you how fast energy is transferred. The time is a separate quantity, and it is the one you divide by.
misconceptions.misconception: Power is basically a measure of time — how long the device takes to do its job.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Time appears in the definition, so students who remember that 'power has something to do with time' may attach the wrong role to it.
misconceptions.correction: Say the definition in full: the rate at which energy is transferred. Rate means 'per second', so time is the divisor, not the answer. To find a time you rearrange to t = E/P.

misconceptions.question: To find the time taken, should power be divided by energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rearranging P = E/t gives t = E/P, so the energy is divided by the power.
misconceptions.misconception: You just swap the two quantities you are given, so t = P/E.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching rather than by algebra, and dividing 'the first number by the second' feels safe.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange properly: multiply both sides by t, then divide by P. Check with units — joules ÷ watts gives seconds, whereas watts ÷ joules does not.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the definition of power?

options.text: The rate at which energy is transferred
options.rationale: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred, or equivalently the rate at which work is done.

options.text: The total energy a device transfers
options.rationale: Students who drop the time from the definition treat power as a quantity of energy rather than a rate.

options.text: The time an energy transfer takes
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember that time appears in the definition but give it the wrong role.

options.text: The force needed to move a load
options.rationale: Confuses power with force; 'powerful' in everyday use suggests strength rather than a rate.

mcqs.stem: Two electric motors lift the same weight through the same height. Motor A takes 4 s and motor B takes 10 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Motor B is more powerful, as it runs for longer
options.rationale: Equates a longer running time with working harder, when a longer time gives a smaller power.

options.text: Motor A is more powerful, as it takes less time
options.rationale: Both motors do the same work, so the one that does it in the shorter time has the greater work done ÷ time.

options.text: The powers are equal, as the work done is equal
options.rationale: Uses only the work done and ignores that the two times differ, which is what decides the power here.

options.text: Motor B is more powerful, as it transfers more energy
options.rationale: Assumes the slower motor must transfer more energy; in fact both transfer the same energy.

mcqs.stem: A kettle transfers 1200 J of energy in 40 s. What is its power?

options.rationale: Comes from multiplying 1200 × 40 instead of dividing.
Comes from subtracting the time from the energy, a slip made when the operation is guessed rather than taken from the equation.
Comes from inverting the fraction and calculating 40 ÷ 1200.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly links power P, energy transferred E and time t?

options.rationale: The multiplication form students reach for when they recall that power involves energy and time but not that it is a rate.
A wrong rearrangement of the correct equation; the correct rearrangement is E = P × t.
Chosen by students who rearrange by swapping symbols rather than by algebra.
This is the specification's symbol form of power = (energy transferred)/(time).

mcqs.stem: A crane does 6000 J of work in 2 minutes. What is its power?

options.rationale: Comes from dividing by 2 minutes without converting the time to seconds.
Comes from converting only one of the two minutes, dividing by 60 s instead of 120 s.
Comes from multiplying the work done by the time in minutes.

mcqs.stem: An electric motor has a power of 500 W. How much energy does it transfer in 30 s?

options.rationale: Comes from dividing 500 by 30 instead of rearranging P = E/t correctly.
Rearranging P = E/t gives E = P × t = 500 × 30 = 15 000 J.
Comes from dividing 30 by 500, the fraction inverted.
Comes from adding the two given values, a slip made when no equation is written down first.

mcqs.stem: In the equation P = E/t, the power P is measured in:

options.rationale: Carries the unit of the energy on the top of the fraction into the answer.
Chosen by students who think power measures how long a transfer lasts.
The specification states power, P, in watts, W.
Confuses power with force, since 'powerful' suggests a large push or pull.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the correct units for using the equation P = E/t?

options.text: E in joules, t in minutes
options.rationale: Chosen by students who never convert a time given in minutes into seconds.

options.text: E in watts, t in seconds
options.rationale: Swaps the units of power and energy, a common consequence of treating the two as the same idea.

options.text: E in newtons, t in seconds
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think energy or work must be measured in the unit of force.

options.text: E in joules, t in seconds
options.rationale: The specification states energy transferred, E, in joules, J and time, t, in seconds, s.

mcqs.stem: A pump does 90 000 J of work in 5 minutes. What is its power?

options.rationale: Comes from dividing by 5 minutes rather than converting the time to 300 s.
Comes from multiplying the work done by the time in minutes.
Comes from inverting the fraction and dividing the time by the work done.

mcqs.stem: In the equation P = W/t, what does W stand for?

options.rationale: Reads W as the unit watt, which is the unit of P and not the quantity on the top line.
The specification states work done, W, in joules, J.
Chosen by students who link W to weight, especially in lifting questions.
Confuses this equation with energy transfers in which some energy is dissipated.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a power of 1 watt is correct?

options.text: It is a total energy transfer of 1 joule
options.rationale: Drops the 'per second', leaving a total energy rather than a rate.

options.text: It transfers 1 joule of energy each minute
options.rationale: Uses minutes instead of seconds, the same slip as failing to convert a time.

options.text: It is an energy transfer of 1 joule each second
options.rationale: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt.

options.text: It is a force of 1 newton acting for 1 second
options.rationale: Confuses power with a force, and sounds plausible because both mention 1 second.

mcqs.stem: Motor X and motor Y lift identical loads through the same height. Motor X takes 2 s and motor Y takes 6 s. How do the work done and the power compare?

options.text: Equal work done; motor Y has three times the power
options.rationale: Gets the work right but assumes the longer-running motor is the more powerful.

options.text: Motor X does three times the work at the same power
options.rationale: Assumes the faster motor must do more work, when the work done is fixed by the lift.

options.text: Motor Y does three times the work and has more power
options.rationale: Assumes a longer job transfers more energy and so gives more power.

options.text: Equal work done; motor X has three times the power
options.rationale: Same load and same height means the same work done; one third of the time gives three times the power.

mcqs.stem: A television transfers 108 000 J of energy in 30 minutes. What is its power?

options.rationale: Comes from dividing by 30 minutes without converting the time to seconds.
Quotes the time in seconds as though it were the answer, a slip made when the final division is not carried out.
Comes from dividing the time by the energy transferred.

mcqs.stem: A washing machine and a hairdryer both transfer 90 000 J of energy. The washing machine runs for 30 minutes and the hairdryer for 5 minutes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The washing machine has greater power, as it runs longer
options.rationale: Treats a longer running time as evidence of greater power.

options.text: The hairdryer has the greater power, as its time is shorter
options.rationale: Equal energy in a shorter time gives a greater rate of transfer: 300 W against 50 W.

options.text: The washing machine has more power, as it uses more energy
options.rationale: Assumes the appliance that runs longer must transfer more energy, though the totals are equal here.

options.text: They have equal power, as the energy transferred is equal
options.rationale: Uses only the energy and ignores the times, which are what differ.

mcqs.stem: A motor transfers 9000 J of energy at a power of 300 W. How long does this take?

options.rationale: Comes from calculating 300 ÷ 9000, the rearrangement done by swapping rather than by algebra.
Comes from multiplying the energy by the power.
Rearranging P = E/t gives t = E/P = 9000/300 = 30 s.
Comes from subtracting the power from the energy, a slip made when no equation is written first.

mcqs.stem: A machine has a power of 250 W and runs for 4 minutes. How much work does it do?

options.rationale: Comes from multiplying by 4 minutes without converting the time to 240 s.
Comes from dividing the power by the time in minutes instead of rearranging correctly.
Quotes the converted time as the answer, a slip made when the multiplication is left undone.
Rearranging P = W/t gives W = P × t = 250 × 240 = 60 000 J.
